blocks.h2: Water Filtration Options for Arlington Heights Homes

tiles.body: Filter every tap in the house, usually for chlorine taste and odor and sediment.
Under-sink reverse osmosis or carbon filters for cooking and drinking water.
Reduce the minerals that leave spots, scale on fixtures and sediment in the water heater.
Catch rust and particles, a common need in homes with older galvanized pipe.

bodies: Arlington Heights gets Lake Michigan water through the Northwest Water Commission, which buys treated water from Evanston. It meets drinking water standards when it leaves the plant. What comes out of your tap also depends on the pipes inside your home.

A water test shows hardness, chlorine, iron and other things that affect taste, scale and appliance life. In older homes, rust from galvanized pipe can show up in the results even when the city water is clean. We use the results to recommend only what your home needs.

blocks.h2: Water Quality in Arlington Heights Homes
blocks.intro: Your water starts in Lake Michigan, but it's the last few hundred feet of pipe that decide what you notice.

items.body: Some homes built in the 1940s through the 1960s still have galvanized supply lines. They rust inside, which can tint the water and reduce pressure. Filtration helps the symptom. [Repiping](/arlington-heights/leak-repairs) fixes the cause.
Treated city water carries a disinfectant all the way to your tap. A carbon filter removes most of the taste and smell.
Lake Michigan water still carries some minerals. If you see white spots on glasses and crust on showerheads, a softener or scale filter may be worth it.

blocks.h2: Water Filtration Questions From Arlington Heights Homeowners

items.q: Is Arlington Heights tap water safe to drink?
items.preview: It meets drinking water standards. Filters improve taste and deal with what your pipes add.
items.answer: The water is treated to meet drinking water standards before it reaches your home. The village publishes a yearly water quality report. A filter improves taste and smell and handles anything your own pipes add.

items.preview: Often old galvanized pipe inside the house.
items.answer: In older Arlington Heights homes, rusty water usually comes from galvanized steel supply pipes corroding from the inside. A sediment filter helps, but replacing the pipe solves it.

items.q: Do I need a water softener with Lake Michigan water?
items.preview: Not always. A test tells you if the minerals are worth treating.
items.answer: Not always. Lake Michigan water carries some hardness minerals. Some homeowners are happy without a softener, others want one for spotless dishes and longer-lasting fixtures. A water test helps you decide.

items.q: How often do filters need changing?
items.preview: It depends on the system. Most cartridges every few months to a year.
items.answer: It depends on the system and your water use. Most cartridges last a few months to a year. We'll set you up with a schedule when we install it.

items.q: How much does a water filtration system cost in Arlington Heights?
items.preview: It depends on the system and installation. You get a flat price first.
items.answer: It depends on the type of system, its size and how it connects to your plumbing. We give you a flat-rate price before any work begins.
